section_summary: This section centers on U.S. efforts to restrict Japan’s access to petroleum technology, aviation gasoline, scrap iron, metals, and other strategic materials during 1940. It documents the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline Company contract dispute, possible indirect transfers of technology through Argentina and Latin America, Japanese procurement in the Netherlands East Indies, and proposals for stronger economic pressure on Japan. The section also contains policy advocacy, intelligence reports, an American Mercury article arguing that the United States could stop Japan economically, internal commentary on that article, and the opening of a statistical study of world war-material exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation with Morito Morishima concerning Universal Oil Products contracts
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Department of State
subfiles.about: Morishima reports Japanese acceptance of a proposed settlement of the 1928 Universal Oil Products contract and discusses possible compromise on the 1938 contract.
subfiles.summary: Morishima says Saneyoshi will withdraw litigation based on the 1928 contract if Universal Oil Products resumes performance, leaving the status of the polymerization process for the companies to resolve. He also proposes separating aviation-gasoline technology from other processes covered by the 1938 contract and asks whether the Japanese Embassy will receive a written reply.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on meeting with H. J. Halle and Healy
subfiles.about: Department officials authorize Universal Oil Products to proceed with its 1928 motor-gasoline cracking-plant contract while withholding action on the 1938 contract.
subfiles.summary: Halle states that he had suspended performance under both contracts while awaiting Department guidance. He agrees to provide plans for motor-gasoline cracking plants under the 1928 agreement and to report when the company and its Japanese counterpart have arranged withdrawal of the associated lawsuit; he will provide nothing under the 1938 agreement without authorization.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Ambassador Grew transmitting Universal Oil Products documents
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Department forwards copies of eight documents concerning the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline Company contracts.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to an earlier March 19 instruction and lists memoranda of conversations from July 9 through August 1. It also includes correspondence from and to Universal Oil Products dated August 8 and August 19.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roger S. Greene to Stanley K. Hornbeck
subfiles.about: Greene sends a policy memorandum advocating stronger economic action against Japan and notes Kurt Bloch’s renewed support for a scrap-iron embargo.
subfiles.summary: Greene states that he has circulated the memorandum to the President, cabinet secretaries, and congressional leaders. He argues that reports of Japanese subsidies for scrap imports suggest that an American embargo would have a meaningful effect.

subfiles.title: The Far Eastern Situation
subfiles.about: The memorandum proposes phased export controls and increased duties as a means of withholding economic support from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene argues that Japan, Germany, and Italy are potential opponents and that concessions would strengthen Japanese action against American and British interests. He recommends licensing iron, steel, copper, scrap metal, petroleum, and vehicles, beginning with a scrap-iron embargo, followed if necessary by delayed or refused licenses and higher duties on Japanese goods. He also advocates financial aid to China.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roger S. Greene to President Franklin D. Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Greene submits his memorandum on a proposed U.S. course of action in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Greene warns that British policies in Burma could aggravate conditions in both the Far East and Europe. He suggests that a just Far Eastern settlement would simplify the defense of the American continent.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roger S. Greene to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Greene sends the Secretary of State his memorandum proposing action in the Far East.
subfiles.summary: The letter repeats Greene’s warning that British concessions in Burma may have harmful consequences beyond Asia. It notes that copies have also gone to the President, the Secretaries of War and Navy, and congressional committee chairmen.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges receipt of Greene’s Far Eastern policy memorandum and covering letters.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Greene for making the memorandum and copies of his letters to the President and Secretary of State available. The reply is a brief formal acknowledgment without substantive policy comment.

subfiles.title: Letter from Roger S. Greene to Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Greene forwards Kurt Bloch’s response to his criticism of Bloch’s views on embargoes against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Greene observes that Bloch remains unconvinced by much of his argument. He emphasizes, however, that new developments have led Bloch to support an embargo on Japanese imports of scrap iron and steel.

subfiles.title: Letter from Kurt Bloch to Roger S. Greene
subfiles.about: Bloch evaluates the likely effectiveness of restricting U.S. strategic exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Bloch argues that Japan could obtain some supplies through transshipment, domestic processing, or alternative sources and that a general embargo would be less effective than earlier in the European war. New Japanese subsidies for scrap imports nevertheless persuade him to favor a scrap-iron embargo or licensing scheme. He also discusses gasoline, copper, lubricants, raw silk duties, scrap rubber, and Japanese stockpiles.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Roger S. Greene concerning Kurt Bloch’s letter
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Greene’s letter and the enclosed copy of Kurt Bloch’s discussion of Far Eastern economic questions.
subfiles.summary: The letter formally records receipt of the material. It offers no substantive response to Bloch’s analysis.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Phillips Petroleum and Argentine petroleum research
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and Division of the American Republics
subfiles.about: The sheet points to memoranda on the danger that aviation-gasoline technology licensed in Argentina might reach Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referenced papers cover discussions with Phillips Petroleum between June 14 and July 2, 1940. The issue was whether a contract with the State Petroleum Company of Argentina could indirectly provide Japan with high-grade aviation-gasoline information.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on R. C. Alden’s inquiry about an Argentine research contract
subfiles.about: A Phillips Petroleum research director asks whether the Department objects to sharing laboratory results, including aviation-gasoline research, with Argentina’s state petroleum company.
subfiles.summary: Alden confirms that the proposed contract would convey important high-quality aviation-gasoline information and concedes that foreign agents might quickly obtain it. Green cites the moral embargo and pending defense legislation and asks the company to submit its question in writing, but Phillips initially declines to do so.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Phillips Petroleum discussions of June 24–25
subfiles.about: Green asks Phillips Petroleum not to conclude its Argentine contract and then learns that it has already been signed.
subfiles.summary: Oberfell explains that negotiations began before the moral embargo and were recently renewed by Villa and Canessa of the Argentine company. The agreement would take effect upon a $250,000 payment on June 29 and provide research information for an additional $250,000. Green refrains from asking Phillips to breach a signed contract without further Department consideration.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Oberfell’s proposal for an industry-wide inquiry
subfiles.about: Oberfell suggests asking other U.S. companies about contracts transferring aviation-gasoline technology to firms in the American republics.
subfiles.summary: Oberfell reasons that the Department’s concern about indirect transfer through Argentina should apply equally to other Latin American agreements. Green replies that he will examine the proposal.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on the Argentine company’s missed payment
subfiles.about: Phillips Petroleum asks for guidance after the Argentine company fails to make the payment needed to activate its contract.
subfiles.summary: Don Emory says the Argentine company has requested a one-month extension but that Phillips is inclined, for business reasons, to let the agreement lapse. Green advises the company to act according to its commercial interests and, after consulting Duggan, plans no further intervention.

subfiles.title: File charge slip for enclosure 1058
subfiles.about: The slip records the temporary charging or circulation of an enclosure associated with file item 1058.
subfiles.summary: The form contains file-handling dates and initials but no substantive discussion of policy. A later 1943 notation also appears on the slip.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese demands for war materials from the Netherlands Indies
subfiles.about: The sheet points to correspondence commenting on Japanese demands for war materials from the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: Only a brief subject description survives in this file. The original correspondence and its date are not legible or supplied on the sheet.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on scrap iron shipped to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a despatch concerning a shipment of scrap iron destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The original was despatch no. 178 from Barranquilla. It was filed elsewhere under number 821.00-N/86.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japan’s requested imports from the Netherlands East Indies
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a memorandum listing commodities demanded by Japan from the Netherlands East Indies.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum originated in the State Department’s Far Eastern division. The original was filed under 756.94/167.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese raw-material negotiations with the Netherlands
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram quoting the Dutch response to Japanese requests for strategic commodities.
subfiles.summary: The listed materials include bauxite, chromium, iron ore, nickel ore, rubber, quinine bark, tin, tin ore, and salt. The referenced original was Grew’s telegram no. 631, filed under 756.94/162.

subfiles.title: Telegram 631 from Tokyo on the Dutch response to Japanese commodity demands
subfiles.about: Grew transmits a translation of the Netherlands minister’s reply concerning Japanese purchases from the Netherlands Indies.
subfiles.summary: The Dutch reply says commercial negotiations are under way for bauxite, chromium, iron ore, nickel ore, rubber, quinine bark, tin, tin ore, and salt, with colonial authorities willing to facilitate agreements. It also addresses castor seeds, scrap iron, wolfram, molybdenum, and manganese, while warning that some minerals are scarce or already fully committed.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Universal Oil Products contract
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a conversation in which the Japanese counselor expressed hope that the Universal Oil Products–Japan Gasoline agreement would be completed.
subfiles.summary: The original memorandum was filed with export-control regulations rather than retained here. The note links the subject to the continuing 1928-contract settlement.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on a Japanese attempt to obtain aircraft equipment through the Dominican Republic
subfiles.from: John A. Butler, U.S. Naval Attaché
subfiles.about: The report investigates a proposal to import aircraft and parts into the Dominican Republic for re-export to Japan.
subfiles.summary: George Burrie says Kiyoshi Mitsutani approached him on behalf of a Japanese traveler identified as Manjo, who reportedly held diplomatic rank and was exploring similar schemes elsewhere in Latin America. The attaché compares the description with travel records for Sakne Manjo and Sabura Nango and notes that success would have required cooperation from senior Dominican officials.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence report translating an anti-American Peiping editorial, with routing notes
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division and Department of State reviewers
subfiles.about: The report forwards an editorial from a Japanese-controlled Peiping newspaper attacking U.S. restrictions on war-material exports.
subfiles.summary: The introductory note identifies the newspaper as an organ of a Japanese-sponsored North China political organization and calls the editorial its first especially virulent attack on America. The translated portion accuses the United States of false neutrality and aiding Britain and France against Germany. Departmental routing annotations indicate that the Controls and Far Eastern divisions had already handled the matter.

subfiles.title: Memorandum authorizing completion of the 1928 Universal Oil Products contract
subfiles.about: Berle directs that Universal Oil Products be told it may complete its cracking-plant contract if the Japanese company withdraws its lawsuit.
subfiles.summary: The decision follows a defense review concluding that completion would not harm national defense. Berle asks that Universal Oil Products and the Japan Gasoline Company be encouraged to work out the settlement directly, with Hamilton available on the details.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on gasoline export restrictions
subfiles.about: Morishima asks how the new aviation-gasoline export regulations affect crude oil and ordinary motor gasoline.
subfiles.summary: Morishima thanks the Department for allowing performance of the 1928 Universal Oil Products contract but says Japanese businessmen are alarmed by the broad technical definition in the July 26 regulations. Yost explains that a plain-language clarification is being prepared. Morishima warns that restrictions on crude petroleum and motor gasoline might cause Japanese importers to reduce U.S. cotton purchases.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the August 5 Morishima–Yost memorandum
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State encloses a copy of the August 5 memorandum of conversation between Morishima and Yost.
subfiles.summary: The brief note formally transmits the record of the discussion on gasoline export restrictions. It contains no additional policy explanation.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Healy’s inquiry about the 1928 contract settlement
subfiles.about: Healy asks whether the Department has approved the attorneys’ agreement to dismiss the lawsuit over the 1928 contract.
subfiles.summary: Moseley says a Department reply has already been drafted and should reach Universal Oil Products shortly. Healy explains that Halle is withholding information until the agreement is approved and confirms that the company will take no action under the 1938 contract without Department instructions.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Canadian lead exports to Japan
subfiles.about: The Canadian chargé reports permits for August lead shipments to Japan and explains Canada’s payment safeguards.
subfiles.summary: Canada authorized export of 4,000 long tons of lead to Japan during August. Mahoney says exporters must obtain irrevocable letters of credit for the full purchase price before shipment and that this policy will continue.

subfiles.title: Letter from Lawrence E. Spivak to Maxwell M. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Spivak sends an advance proof of Robert Aura Smith’s article “We Can Stop Japan.”
subfiles.summary: Spivak describes Smith as an experienced Far Eastern correspondent then serving on the New York Times editorial staff. He calls the article timely and documented and asks for Hamilton’s comments.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Spivak’s letter and article
subfiles.about: Ballantine acknowledges receipt of the advance proof of “We Can Stop Japan.”
subfiles.summary: The division has read the article with interest and will bring it to Hamilton’s attention when he returns. Ballantine thanks Spivak for making the proof available.

subfiles.title: Advance proof of “We Can Stop Japan”
subfiles.doc_type: magazine article and accompanying proof pages
subfiles.about: Smith argues that U.S. economic leverage could halt Japanese aggression without waiting for overwhelming military strength.
subfiles.summary: The article contends that American exports of petroleum, scrap iron, copper, machinery, and other materials sustain Japan’s military operations while raw-silk sales provide Japan with essential foreign exchange. Smith emphasizes Japan’s dependence on the United States, its strained budget and domestic shortages, and its vulnerability to a total oil embargo and a scrap-iron embargo. He also proposes a stronger naval presence in the South China Sea, while the final proof pages include incidental magazine material following the article.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary’s routing memorandum to Hornbeck
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Under Secretary’s office forwards material concerning the American Mercury article for information and acknowledgment.
subfiles.summary: The note is an internal routing instruction rather than a substantive policy paper. It directs Hornbeck to review and acknowledge the enclosed material.

subfiles.title: Letter from Lawrence E. Spivak to Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Spivak sends Welles an advance proof of Robert Aura Smith’s “We Can Stop Japan.”
subfiles.summary: The letter duplicates the information sent to Hamilton about Smith’s Far Eastern experience and forthcoming book, Our Future in Asia. Spivak again describes the article as timely and well documented and invites comment.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Lawrence E. Spivak on behalf of Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Hornbeck thanks Spivak for sending Welles the American Mercury article.
subfiles.summary: Welles has read the article with interest and appreciates Spivak’s courtesy. Hornbeck also notes the forthcoming publication of Smith’s book Our Future in Asia.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck memorandum on “We Can Stop Japan”
subfiles.about: Hornbeck broadly endorses Smith’s argument but questions sending major U.S. fleet units into the South China Sea.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck argues that determined, sustained economic pressure could stop Japan without necessarily producing war with the United States. He believes moves into French Indochina or the Netherlands East Indies would overextend Japan, create new enemies, expose vulnerable naval lines, and hasten the failure of its imperial program. He concludes that U.S. policy should not be constrained by fear of Japanese adventurism, though he doubts Smith’s naval-deployment proposal.

subfiles.title: Letter from Frederick C. McKee to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: McKee forwards current articles on Japan, highlighting a recent Lippmann column.
subfiles.summary: McKee believes the enclosed Lippmann column is especially significant because it contrasts with an earlier column favoring appeasement of Japan. The referenced clippings are not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: Reply from Cordell Hull to Frederick C. McKee
subfiles.about: Hull thanks McKee for sending several press clippings.
subfiles.summary: Hull says he anticipates examining the material with interest. He expresses appreciation for McKee’s courtesy in forwarding it.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on a war-materials item
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to an original document concerning Japan and war-material exports, but most identifying text is illegible in the OCR.
subfiles.summary: The surviving page is a records-office pointer rather than the original document. Its source, date, recipient, and precise subject cannot be recovered confidently from the supplied text.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on possible Mexican scrap-iron sales to Japan
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram warning that Mexico would solicit bids for 150,000 tons of scrap iron that might be sold to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Finance Minister Suárez was reportedly scheduled to receive bids on September 3. Daniels requested immediate guidance if the Department wished to prevent a Japanese purchase.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese preference in nickel supplies
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram reporting that the Pétain government had ordered preferential treatment for Japan in nickel supplies.
subfiles.summary: The original information appeared in telegram no. 17 from Australia. It was filed with records on the European war rather than retained in this subject file.

subfiles.title: World Exports to Japan Essential for War Purposes, 1937–39
subfiles.about: The opening of Bulletin No. 12 analyzes the countries and commodities supplying Japan with materials essential for war.
subfiles.summary: The bulletin’s contents outline commodity, geographic, and political-group analyses together with extensive statistical appendices. Its opening analysis estimates 1939 war-material shipments to Japan at $292.075 million, about half of Japanese imports, with petroleum, iron materials, metal-working machinery, and copper comprising nearly seventy percent of the total. Tables compare the composition and value of these exports in 1937, 1938, and 1939.
